blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — acute-care MRSA Contact Precautions and discontinuation without a universal national endpoint
stem: An acute-care inpatient is colonized with MRSA and is on Contact Precautions. The family asks when the precautions can be stopped. Which explanation is most accurate?

options.A: Continue Contact Precautions for acute-care MRSA colonization and use the facility infection-prevention policy to determine when they can be discontinued.
options.B: Discontinue Contact Precautions after one negative nasal screen if the client has no active MRSA infection, because a single result establishes clearance.
options.C: Discontinue Contact Precautions once fever and drainage are absent for 24 hours, because symptom resolution defines the national endpoint for MRSA isolation.
options.D: Use Standard Precautions alone for colonization without infection, reserving Contact Precautions for clients with active MRSA disease or draining wounds.

rationale: A is correct. Current CDC MRSA infection-control guidance, dated June 27, 2025, recommends Contact Precautions in inpatient acute-care settings for patients colonized or infected with MRSA. CDC's current MDRO Summary of Recommendations, dated March 18, 2024, separately states that no recommendation can be made regarding when to discontinue Contact Precautions because this remains an unresolved issue. Therefore the nurse should not apply a universal fever-free period, a single-negative-culture rule, or an infection-only rule; discontinuation should follow the facility's infection-prevention policy and applicable local requirements. B is incorrect because CDC does not identify one negative nasal screen as a universal national clearance criterion. C is incorrect because symptom resolution does not establish a national discontinuation endpoint for MRSA colonization. D is incorrect because CDC specifically recommends Contact Precautions in acute care for MRSA-colonized as well as infected patients.
educational_objective: Recognize that acute-care MRSA colonization remains an indication for Contact Precautions and that CDC does not define one universal national discontinuation criterion; follow the facility infection-prevention policy rather than inventing a fixed culture or symptom endpoint.

option_audit.A: Correct; integrates CDC's acute-care MRSA Contact Precautions recommendation with the absence of a universal national discontinuation endpoint.
option_audit.B: Plausible screening-based rule; incorrect because one negative nasal screen is not a CDC universal national criterion for discontinuation.
option_audit.C: Plausible symptom-based rule; incorrect because CDC does not define a fever/drainage-free period as the national endpoint for MRSA Contact Precautions.
option_audit.D: Plausible infection-versus-colonization distinction; incorrect because CDC recommends Contact Precautions for acute-care patients who are colonized as well as infected.
